> **What this case shows** — a power spectrum tells you *which* rhythms are present but
> not *when* — and brain rhythms come and go. The **Morlet-wavelet transform** keeps both
> axes: it convolves the signal with a family of wavelets, one per frequency, to build a
> time-frequency **scalogram**. On a real eyes-closed occipital recording the scalogram
> shows the story unambiguously — a band of power sitting at **10 Hz** across the whole
> segment: the **alpha rhythm** Berger discovered, resolved in time and frequency, with
> **66%** of the scalogram's power in the 8–13 Hz alpha band. And the transform is
> trustworthy: the ecosystem's `waveletTransform` reproduces MNE-Python's
> `tfr_array_morlet` — the field-standard — in time-frequency **structure** to a
> correlation of **0.9998** (full scalogram) and **0.9999** (time-averaged spectrum), the
> two differing only by a constant normalization factor.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — for a time-frequency picture: `waveletTransform(pe, frequencies, n_cycles)`
→ read the **scalogram** (power over time × frequency) → find where the power lives.
**Way of thinking** — a scalogram trades a little frequency resolution for *timing*:
`n_cycles` sets that trade-off (more cycles = sharper frequency, blurrier time). Use it
when *when* matters — event-related power, bursts — not for a static spectrum.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioAnalysis::waveletTransform()`, and `crossWaveletTransform()`
/ `waveletCoherence()` for transient coupling between channels.
:::

## Proposition

On real eyes-closed occipital EEG (eegmmidb S001R02, O1), the Morlet scalogram peaks at
10 Hz (66% of power in the alpha band), and `waveletTransform` reproduces MNE
`tfr_array_morlet` in structure (correlation 0.9998 / 0.9999).

## Question & goal

**The question is whether the ecosystem paints the same time-frequency picture as the
field-standard tool.** A scalogram is only useful if the transform is right, and Morlet
implementations differ in normalization and edge handling. The goal is a head-to-head
against MNE `tfr_array_morlet`, and a clear read: does the occipital scalogram show alpha?

## Challenge & approach

The Morlet transform convolves the signal with complex wavelets at each frequency; the
result's magnitude-squared is the scalogram. We compute it with `waveletTransform` and
with MNE, matched on frequencies and `n_cycles`, and compare the two time-frequency maps.

```
O1 EEG → waveletTransform (Morlet, 4-30 Hz, 7 cycles) → scalogram
                                                        vs MNE tfr_array_morlet
                                                        → structure correlation + alpha peak
```

## Data

**eegmmidb — EEG Motor Movement/Imagery Database (PhysioNet)**: subject S001, baseline run
**R02 (eyes-closed rest)**, occipital channel **O1**, first 10 s at 160 Hz — the same EDF
the sibling `eeg-alpha` / `eeg-aperiodic` cases read. Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

Right: the time-averaged marginal spectrum — waveletTransform (red) and MNE tfr_array_morlet (blue, scaled) sit on top of each other, both peaking sharply at 10 Hz.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* the scalogram's bright horizontal band is the ongoing alpha rhythm;
the right panel confirms the two tools produce the same spectral shape (the scale factor
is a normalization convention).

| Quantity | This reproduction | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Dominant frequency | **10 Hz** (alpha) | — |
| Alpha-band power fraction | **0.66** | — |
| Full-TFR correlation vs MNE | **0.9998** | 1 (same structure) |
| Marginal-spectrum correlation | **0.9999** | 1 |
| Normalization scale (op/MNE) | 0.49 | convention |

The scalogram is alpha-dominated and matches MNE's structure almost perfectly. Values
trace to [`artifacts/wavelet_summary.csv`](artifacts/wavelet_summary.csv) and the marginal
spectrum in
[`artifacts/wavelet_marginal_spectrum.csv`](artifacts/wavelet_marginal_spectrum.csv).

## Conclusion

The ecosystem's Morlet scalogram is the same time-frequency picture MNE paints — down to a
normalization constant — and it shows the occipital alpha rhythm plainly. The transferable
takeaway: **use the wavelet scalogram when timing matters, validate its structure against
the field-standard tool, and remember that Morlet normalization is a convention — compare
shapes and correlations, not absolute power, across implementations.**

## Open questions

- The scalogram's strength is **timing**: an event-related design (eyes-open/closed
  transitions, a task) would show alpha appearing and disappearing, and a **cross-wavelet**
  or **wavelet-coherence** analysis (`crossWaveletTransform` / `waveletCoherence`, also
  implemented) would track transient coupling between channels. Extending this static
  demonstration to event-related time-frequency — and pinning the normalization to MNE's
  exactly — would turn a validated transform into a dynamics study. *Documented, not
  escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| Morlet scalogram (time-frequency) | `waveletTransform()` | PhysioAnalysis |
| cross-wavelet (two signals) | `crossWaveletTransform()` | PhysioAnalysis |
| wavelet coherence | `waveletCoherence()` | PhysioCrossModal |
| the aperiodic 1/f background (context) | `eegAperiodic()` | PhysioEEG |

**Choosing the parameters.**

- **frequencies** — the frequencies to resolve (here 4–30 Hz, step 2); denser gives a
  smoother scalogram at more cost.
- **n_cycles** — the time-frequency trade-off: 7 cycles (used here) is a common default;
  fewer cycles sharpen timing but blur frequency, more do the reverse. It can be a vector
  (more cycles at higher frequencies).
- **normalization** — `"L2"` / `"L1"`; the absolute power scale is a convention, so
  compare shapes across tools, not raw magnitudes.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioAnalysis)

wt <- waveletTransform(pe, frequencies = seq(4, 30, by = 2), n_cycles = 7)
P  <- wt$power                                   # power[frequency, time] -- the scalogram
wt$frequencies[which.max(rowMeans(P))]           # 10 Hz -- the dominant (alpha) rhythm

# reproduces MNE's tfr_array_morlet in structure (correlation ~0.9998), up to a
# normalization convention.
```
